---
name: backtest
description: Turn a plain-English trading idea into a strategy file for the qbt backtester in the sp500-data repo, run it against the point-in-time S&P 500 / ETF dataset (1970–today), and report the results honestly against SPY. Use whenever John describes a strategy to test ("backtest X", "what if I bought ... and sold ...", "test this rule", "/backtest"), asks to change or re-run one, or asks to sweep a parameter. Not for data-quality work on the dataset itself.
---

# /backtest — custom strategy backtests

John describes what he wants in plain English. You write the Python, run it,
and tell him what happened. He is not a coder: never ask him to edit code or
run commands.

## 1. Set up (once per session)

```bash
# repo not present?  attach it with the add_repo tool, then:
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/Johnbrick123/sp500-data /home/claude/sp500-data
pip install -q pandas pyarrow duckdb numpy --break-system-packages
cd /home/claude/sp500-data && python backtest.py strategies/momentum_15.py --quiet --no-report
```
The first run downloads the release data (~235 MB) and builds the panel cache.
Then read `docs/BACKTEST_API.md` — it is the whole API.

## 2. Translate the idea into a strategy file

Write `strategies/<short_slug>.py` with one `Strategy` subclass. The docstring
restates his request in plain English; `name` is a short human title.

Map his words to the API:
- "rotate / rebalance monthly" → `schedule = "monthly"`, rank, `ctx.equal_weight(ctx.top(score, n))`
- "hold until ..." / "sell when ..." → keep `ctx.portfolio.holdings` that still pass the sell test, refill freed slots, `ctx.hold(book, rebalance=False)` if he wants winners to run
- "stop loss / trailing stop / exit after N days" → `on_day` with `ctx.sell(t)`
- "only when the market is above its 200-day" → `ctx.price_to_sma(200, tickers=["SPY"])["SPY"] > 0`
- "weight by inverse vol" → `ctx.inverse_vol_weight(...)`
- "ETFs" → `universe = "etfs"` or an explicit list; sector ETF menu lives in `strategies/etf_rotation.py`
- "since 19xx" → `start`; signals still use all prior history
- costs unstated → 10 bps (5 for ETFs); start unstated → 2010-01-01; weighting unstated → equal

Decide defaults yourself and state them in the write-up. Ask at most one
question, and only if the answer changes the result materially (e.g. he says
"sell when it breaks down" with no definition). Otherwise pick the sensible
reading and say what you picked.

Before running, check the strategy against the data's limits
(`docs/BACKTEST_API.md` → Mechanics): no open/high/low/volume before 1996,
SPY from 1995, membership from 1970.

## 3. Run

```bash
cd /home/claude/sp500-data
python backtest.py strategies/<slug>.py --quiet
```
Read `results/<name>/summary.txt`, `yearly.csv`, and `log.txt` (delistings,
stop-outs). If the run errors, fix the strategy file and rerun — do not hand
the error to John.

Cheap robustness checks worth running when the result looks good:
- `--sweep cost_bps=5,10,20,35` (does the edge survive real-world costs?)
- `--start 1997-01-01` and `--start 2010-01-01` (does it depend on the window?)
- the main parameter ±: `--sweep n=10,15,20,30`

## 4. Report back (chat, mobile-sized)

Lead with the verdict in one sentence, then a compact table: CAGR, Sharpe,
max drawdown, worst year, turnover — strategy vs SPY. Then 3–5 plain-English
findings, including the honest risks: which years carry the return, what
costs do to it, turnover/tax implications, data-coverage caveats for
pre-1996 runs. He values honest risk disclosure next to the bull case.

Publish `results/<name>/report.html` as an Artifact (it is self-contained) so
he can open it on his phone. Do not paste the URL; the card carries it.

## 5. Keep the record

```bash
git add strategies/<slug>.py docs/strategy-log.md
git commit -m "backtest: <name>" && git push
```
Append a dated entry to `docs/strategy-log.md`: the plain-English rule, the
headline numbers vs SPY, and the verdict. Results folders are git-ignored;
the strategy file and the log are the record. If `claude/backtester.md` in
the Claude Project exists, add the same entry there.

## Changing the engine

If an idea needs something the API lacks (a new indicator, a new order type),
add it to `qbt/indicators.py` or `qbt/engine.py`, keep it general, document
it in `docs/BACKTEST_API.md`, and commit it. The engine is his, not a vendor's.

docs_md.README.md:
# S&P 500 + ETF Historical Dataset

Free, reproducible, point-in-time S&P 500 history: who was in the index on
every trading day since **1970**, with a price for every one of them on every
day, plus ETFs. No paid data vendor.

> **Read this first.** Two tiers, checked differently (details in the
> verification log):
> - **1996 to today** — every member priced on every day, every close and
>   dividend cross-checked against CRSP and at least one vendor or archive,
>   membership matched to S&P's own announcements.
> - **1970–1995** — membership from CRSP's own S&P 500 list and prices from
>   CRSP (no free vendor carries the companies that disappeared before
>   1996). Checked against the published S&P 500 (the index rebuilt from
>   these members tracks it within ~3–5 basis points a day), against CRSP's
>   own returns, and against Yahoo for the 174 survivors. No
>   open/high/low/volume.
>
> **Every member-day from 1970 to 2024 is compared with CRSP's daily total
> return** (`tools/full_crsp_check.py`, published as `full_check_*` files).
> Disagreements over 0.5pp go to the published S&P 500's own daily return,
> which decides when the member is big enough. Results:
> - 99.990% of 6,943,082 member-days are within 0.5pp. The 669 that are not are
>   listed in `full_check_flagged.csv`.
> - Where the index can judge, it never sides with CRSP against this data: 12 runs
>   favour ours, and the other 333 are too small or too close to call (mostly
>   1995–2004 fractional-price closes, where CRSP and the vendors print
>   different eighths).
> - Dividends are tested by each label-year's summed difference: 100 of the 28,710
>   label-years drift more than 0.1pp, each listed in `full_check_drift.csv`.
>
> **Two files to use in any backtest:**
> - `no_trade_days.csv` lists the 3,019 member-days that are not trades:
>   halts, suspensions and CRSP's missing days, carried at the prior close
>   (source `carried-patch`). Don't trade on them. Don't read their zero
>   return as a calm day: a low-volatility screen would otherwise pick a
>   suspended stock.
> - `exit_gaps.csv` lists removals whose last member day was not a trade:
>   SVB and Signature Bank 2023, HealthSouth 2003 and five 1970s companies.
>   A holder could not sell at that close. Book the next trade instead:
>   SVB −99.6% and Signature −99.8% on 3/28/2023.

## What you have

| | |
|---|---|
| Rows | 12,285,625 |
| Tickers | 1,895 (1,742 that were ever index members) |
| Prices | 1968-01-02 → today (nightly) |
| Membership | 1970-01-02 → today, 500-505 members every day |
| Size | 235 MB (Parquet) |

`data/prices.parquet` — one tidy table (`close` is as its `source` stores it — Yahoo's is split-adjusted, Tiingo's, WIKI's and CRSP's are as traded — so use `adj_close`, split+dividend adjusted, for returns): `date, ticker, open, high, low, close, volume, adj_close, dividends, stock_splits, source`

## Run it

```bash
pip install yfinance pandas pyarrow duckdb

python build_universe.py     # ticker universe + point-in-time membership
python bridge_membership.py  # extend membership 2019 -> today, normalize renames
python fetch_prices.py       # pull raw OHLCV + corporate actions (resumable)
python fetch_delisted_tiingo.py   # optional: recover delisted names (needs free key)
python compute_adjusted.py   # derive our own adjusted prices
python verify.py             # 8 independent data-quality checks
python build_db.py           # load into DuckDB (local)
python load_motherduck.py    # or push to MotherDuck (online, free tier)
```

`fetch_prices.py` is resumable and incremental — re-running only fetches what's
missing. A full cold backfill takes ~20 minutes. A nightly update takes seconds.

## Three things that will bite you (and what was done about them)

**1. Survivorship bias.** 1,742 companies have been in the S&P 500 since 1970;
503 are in it today. A "current members" dataset silently deletes the rest and
will flatter every backtest you run.

*Handled:* `membership_intervals.parquet` holds [start, end) spans per label
(dead companies carry a `-YYYYMM` suffix), and every member has a price on
every day it was a member — the dead ones recovered from Tiingo, Quandl's WIKI
file, archives and, for most of them, CRSP. The `v_sp500` view joins prices to
those spans.

**2. Yahoo's `Adj Close` is unstable.** It gets silently restated every time a
new dividend posts, so last month's snapshot won't reproduce today.

*Handled:* we store raw OHLCV plus a separate corporate-actions record and
derive `adj_close` ourselves in `compute_adjusted.py`. Same inputs always give
the same outputs — your backtests become reproducible.

**3. Ticker recycling.** When a company is acquired or delisted, its symbol gets
reassigned to an unrelated company. Example found in this data: **STI** was
SunTrust Banks, an S&P 500 bank that merged into Truist in 2019. Yahoo purged
SunTrust's history, and STI now returns a ~$6 microcap with data starting 2022.
Join that to the membership table and you're backtesting the wrong company
entirely — silently, with no error.

*Handled:* check 7 in `verify.py` flags any ticker whose price history begins
after it left the index. **17 found**, listed in `data/recycled_tickers.csv`.
Exclude them from point-in-time work.

## Verification (`verify.py`)

1. **Split spot-checks** — AAPL 7:1 and 4:1, NVDA 10:1, TSLA 5:1, AMZN/GOOGL 20:1
2. **Cross-source** — Stooq vs Yahoo adjusted returns
3. **Calendar** — duplicate, weekend, and missing rows
4. **Outliers** — >25% daily moves with no matching corporate action
5. **Continuity** — gaps longer than 10 calendar days
6. **Index reconstruction** — equal-weight large-cap basket vs SPY
7. **Recycled tickers** — symbol reassignment detection
8. **Adjustment reconciliation** — our derived total return vs Yahoo's

Every check reports PASS, FAIL or UNVERIFIED. A check that cannot run
(source unreachable, sample missing) is UNVERIFIED and never counted as a pass.

### Why check 8 exists

The first build had a bug: Yahoo's `Close` column is *already* split-adjusted,
so dividing by the split ratio again double-counted it. SPY and XOM looked
perfect (no splits since 2005) while AAPL was off by 56x.

The damage it did to check 6 is the real lesson — the 20-name basket showed
**18.33% CAGR against SPY's 14.08%.** Over 4% a year of pure phantom alpha,
from a data bug, in names you'd never suspect. After the fix: 14.18% vs 14.08%,
correlation 0.91.

That is the entire argument for running verification before you trust a
backtest. The bug was invisible in the price series and obvious in the returns.

## Known limitations — read before trusting a backtest

- **Before 1996 the data rests on CRSP** (see the top of this file), with
  Yahoo as a second source only for the companies that still trade under
  their own symbol. The 1996-onward years were verified day by day against
  several sources.
- **2025 and 2026 are not in the CRSP check** (the free CRSP file ends in
  December 2024). Instead:
  - Every member's daily return is audited against Nasdaq. Two days differed
    in 2025–26, and both are now explained and booked.
  - The ETFs are audited the same way.
  - Dividends of the Nasdaq-listed members match Nasdaq's record exactly.
  - An equal-weight rebuild tracks RSP within the range of the CRSP-checked
    years.

  Two gaps remain:
  - Dividends of the NYSE-listed members have no second source until
    Tiingo's monthly allowance resets (November 2026).
  - Twelve companies acquired in 2025–26 (about 2,000 member-days) rest on
    Tiingo alone.
- **Dividends use the total-return convention**: the ex-date return is
  (close + dividend) / previous close − 1, which is CRSP's and S&P's
  convention. Since 2026-10-16 this replaces Yahoo's formula, which was off
  by about the yield times the day's move. `adj_close` therefore differs
  slightly from Yahoo's adjusted close on ex-dividend days.
- **Membership 2019 -> today is replayed from Wikipedia's change log**
  (`bridge_membership.py`). Wikipedia dropped that table from the live page in
  mid-2026, so the script reads it from an older page revision. Renamed symbols
  (FB->META, ANTM->ELV, 37 total in `renames.csv`) are normalized to the symbol
  Yahoo keeps the history under, which recovered those names for free.
- **Most ETFs don't go back 25 years.** SPY (1993), MDY (1995), DIA (1998),
  QQQ and the sector SPDRs (1998–99) do. Most others start 2003–2010. Splicing
  in index history before inception is a modeling choice — make it deliberately.
- **yfinance is an unofficial scraper.** Yahoo can change or throttle the
  endpoints at any time. The fetcher batches 25 tickers per request with a
  1-second pause to stay clear of rate limits.

## Online access (all free)

**MotherDuck** — DuckDB hosted in the cloud. `load_motherduck.py` pushes the
tables; then `duckdb.connect('md:market')` from any machine, or use their web
SQL editor. Every query in this repo runs unchanged.

**GitHub Releases** — `.g
docs_md.SETUP.md:
# Setup — about 5 minutes, all free

The database is a public GitHub repo. GitHub Actions refreshes the data every
weeknight and publishes it as a Release asset at a fixed URL. Anyone with the
URL — you, a colleague, Claude — queries it directly with DuckDB. No server,
no account needed to read, nothing to pay.

## 1. Create the repo
GitHub → New repository → name it (e.g. `sp500-data`) → **Public** → Create.

Public is what makes this work: reading needs no token, so Claude can query it
in any session and a colleague needs only the link. The data is Yahoo-derived
daily prices — nothing proprietary. (A private repo works too, but then every
reader needs a token, including Claude, every time.)

## 2. Upload the files
Unzip `sp500-dataset-pipeline.zip` and upload everything to the repo
(drag-and-drop on the GitHub website works; `.github/workflows/update.yml`
must keep its folder path).

## 3. Optional secrets  (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions)
- `TIINGO_API_KEY` — free key from tiingo.com. Recovers the ~588 delisted
  companies Yahoo purged. Strongly recommended for backtesting.
- `MOTHERDUCK_TOKEN` — only if you also want a hosted SQL console.

## 4. Run it once
Actions tab → "Nightly market data update" → Run workflow. First run is the
full 20-minute backfill; every night after that takes a couple of minutes.
It then runs itself, weekdays at 6 pm Chicago.

## 5. Share it
The data URL is stable and public:

    https://github.com/<you>/<repo>/releases/download/data/prices.parquet

Send that to a colleague with `query_remote.py`, or the repo link. To give a
colleague edit rights: Settings → Collaborators.

Send the repo URL to Claude and it can query the live data in any conversation.

# qbt — the backtester

A QuantConnect-style engine for the `sp500-data` dataset. You describe a
strategy as a short Python class; the engine walks every trading day from
1970 to today, fills your orders, charges costs, marks the book daily on
total returns, and writes a one-page report.

```
python backtest.py strategies/momentum_15.py                    # run it
python backtest.py strategies/momentum_15.py --start 1990-01-01 # different window
python backtest.py strategies/momentum_15.py --set n=20 --set cost_bps=20
python backtest.py strategies/momentum_15.py --sweep cost_bps=5,10,20,35
```

Output: `results/<name>/report.html` plus `equity.csv`, `trades.csv`,
`round_trips.csv`, `holdings.csv`, `yearly.csv`, `summary.json`, `log.txt`.

First run downloads the release data (~235 MB) and builds the panel cache
(~10 s). After that a 17-year monthly strategy runs in about 3 seconds; a
daily strategy in 10–20 seconds; the full 1970–2026 record in under 10.

## Anatomy of a strategy

```python
from qbt import Strategy

class Momentum15(Strategy):
    name = "Momentum 15"
    start = "2010-01-01"      # None = 1970
    end = None                # None = latest day
    schedule = "monthly"      # when on_rebalance runs
    cost_bps = 10             # per side
    n = 15                    # any extra attribute becomes a parameter (--set n=20)

    def on_rebalance(self, ctx):
        score = (0.4 * ctx.momentum(252, 21) + 0.3 * ctx.momentum(126, 21)
                 + 0.2 * ctx.momentum(63, 21) + 0.1 * ctx.pct_of_high(252))
        ctx.equal_weight(ctx.top(score, self.n))
```

Three hooks, all optional except `on_rebalance`:

| hook | runs | use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `initialize(self)` | once, before the first day | set up state (`self.highs = {}`) |
| `on_rebalance(self, ctx)` | on every schedule day | ranking, buying, selling |
| `on_day(self, ctx)` | every trading day | stops, circuit breakers, daily checks |

## Settings (class attributes)

| setting | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `start`, `end` | `"2010-01-01"`, `None` | test window; signals still use all history before `start` |
| `cash` | 1,000,000 | starting capital |
| `schedule` | `"monthly"` | `"daily"`, `"weekly"`, `"monthly"`, `"quarterly"`, `"annual"`, a list of dates, or a function `f(date) -> bool` |
| `schedule_when` | `"end"` | `"end"` = last trading day of the period, `"start"` = first |
| `entry_lag` | 1 | fill N trading days after the signal day (0 = same close) |
| `fill` | `"close"` | `"close"` or `"open"` (open prices exist from 1996) |
| `cost_bps` | 10 | commission + spread per side |
| `slippage_bps` | 0 | extra adverse move on every fill |
| `cash_rate` | 0.0 | annual interest earned on idle cash |
| `benchmark` | `"SPY"` | any ticker, or `None` (SPY prices begin Jan 1995) |
| `universe` | `"sp500"` | `"sp500"` (point-in-time members), `"etfs"`, `"all"`, or a list of tickers |
| `min_history` | 0 | days of prices a name needs before it is eligible |
| `min_dollar_volume` | 0 | 63-day median dollar volume floor |
| `sell_if_not_eligible` | False | auto-sell names that drop out of the universe |
| `buy_order_ttl` | 5 | days an unfilled buy is retried before it is dropped |

## What `ctx` gives you on a day

Everything is **point-in-time**: values are as of `ctx.date`, computed from
trailing data only. There is no way to read tomorrow.

### Universe
- `ctx.date`, `ctx.i` — today
- `ctx.universe` — eligible tickers today (list)
- `ctx.sp500` — S&P 500 members today, regardless of the strategy universe
- `ctx.etfs` — the ETF set
- `ctx.in_index(t)`, `ctx.tradable(t)`

### Prices
- `ctx.price("AAPL")` → float; `ctx.price()` → Series over the universe
- `ctx.price(field="close")` for raw `close`, `open`, `high`, `low`, `volume`, `dividends`
- `ctx.history("adj_close", days=252)` → DataFrame of the last 252 rows (dates × tickers); `tickers=[...]` to narrow

### Indicators (Series over the universe; `tickers=[...]` to narrow; `days=N` for a DataFrame of history)
| call | meaning |
|---|---|
| `ctx.returns(63)` | trailing 63-day total return |
| `ctx.momentum(252, 21)` | return from 252 days ago to 21 days ago (the "12-1") |
| `ctx.sma(200)`, `ctx.ema(50)` | moving averages |
| `ctx.price_to_sma(200)` | price / SMA − 1 (> 0 means above) |
| `ctx.above_sma(200, buffer=0.02)` | boolean: price > SMA × 1.02 |
| `ctx.pct_of_high(252)` | price / 52-week high (1.0 = at the high) |
| `ctx.rolling_high(252)`, `ctx.rolling_low(252)` | trailing extremes |
| `ctx.drawdown()` | distance from all-time high |
| `ctx.volatility(63)` | annualised vol of daily returns |
| `ctx.atr(14)` | average true range (1996+) |
| `ctx.dollar_volume(63)` | median daily $ volume |
| `ctx.rsi(14)` | RSI |
| `ctx.macd(12, 26, 9)` | MACD histogram |
| `ctx.monthly_macd(8, 17, 9)` | MACD histogram on month-end closes |
| `ctx.zscore(20)`, `ctx.bollinger_pct(20, 2)` | mean-reversion measures |
| `ctx.days_of_history()` | how many priced days a name has |
| `ctx.indicator("name", ...)` | any function in `qbt/indicators.py` |

Add a new indicator by writing a function in `qbt/indicators.py` decorated
with `@cached` that returns a DataFrame computed with rolling/trailing windows.

### Ranking helpers
- `ctx.top(score, 15)` — 15 highest; `ascending=True` for lowest
- `ctx.where(cond)` — tickers where a boolean Series is True
- `ctx.rank(score)`

### Portfolio
- `ctx.portfolio.holdings` (list), `.weights` (Series), `.weight(t)`, `.has(t)`
- `.value`, `.cash`, `.invested` (fraction)
- `.pnl_pct(t)` since entry, `.days_held(t)`, `.entry_date(t)`, `.price(t)`

### Orders (target weights of portfolio value, filled `entry_lag` days later)
- `ctx.set_weights({"AAPL": .5, "MSFT": .5})` — the whole book; anything not named is sold
- `ctx.equal_weight(tickers, total=1.0)`
- `ctx.inverse_vol_weight(tickers, window=63)`
- `ctx.hold(tickers, rebalance=False)` — keep these names; `rebalance=False` lets winners run instead of trimming to equal weight
- `ctx.buy(t, weight)` / `ctx.target(t, weight)` — change one name, leave the rest
- `ctx.sell(t)`, `ctx.liquidate()`
- weights that sum to less than 1 leave the rest in cash

### Diagnostics
- `ctx.log("text")` → `log.txt`
- `ctx.record(cash_pct=0.2)` → `result.records` DataFrame

## Mechanics you should know

- **Fills.** Orders placed on day *d* fill at the close (or open) of day
  *d + entry_lag*. A name that is not tradable that day is retried daily (sells
  indefinitely, buys for `buy_order_ttl` days).
- **Marking.** Daily, on `adj_close` (split- and dividend-adjusted total
  return). Drawdowns are real daily drawdowns, not rebalance-to-rebalance.
- **Costs.** `cost_bps` on every dollar traded, each side. Delisting exits pay it too.
- **Delistings.** When a holding stops trading it is closed at its last real
  trade. For the companies in `exit_gaps.csv` (SVB, Signature, HealthSouth …)
  the next trade price is used instead: you could not have sold at the last
  close. Every such exit is in `log.txt`.
- **No-trade days** (`no_trade_days.csv`) are never fill days and never count
  as a trading opportunity; the strategy still sees the carried price.
- **Index membership** is point-in-time. A name that leaves the index stays
  in the book until the strategy sells it (or `sell_if_not_eligible = True`).
- **Before 1996** only closes exist: `open/high/low/volume`, `atr`,
  `dollar_volume` and `fill = "open"` are empty there.
- **Statistics.** CAGR is geometric. Sharpe and Sortino use the annualised
  arithmetic mean of daily returns over the annualised standard deviation
  (risk-free rate 0). Turnover = one-way traded value / average equity / year.

## Running from Python

```python
from qbt import run_file
res = run_file("strategies/momentum_15.py", n=20, start="2000-01-01")
print(res.summary())
res.stats["strategy"]["cagr"]; res.equity; res.trades; res.holdings
```

## Describing a strategy in plain English

You do not need to write the Python. Say what you want and Claude turns it
into a strategy file using this API, runs it, and reports back. The things to
specify (defaults in brackets):

1. **Universe** — S&P 500 [default], ETFs, or a list
2. **When to act** — monthly [default], weekly, daily, quarterly, annual
3. **What to buy** — the rule or ranking (momentum, low vol, RSI, above the 200-day …)
4. **How many / how to weight** — top 15 equal weight [default], inverse vol, let winners run
5. **When to sell** — rotate out of the top N [default], or a sell rule, stop, time limit
6. **Costs, start date, cash rate** — 10 bps, 2010, 0% [defaults]

Example: *"Buy the 20 S&P 500 stocks with the best 6-month return that are
above their 200-day average. Rebalance quarterly. Sell anything that falls
15% from its high. Run it from 1990 at 15 bps."*

# Strategy log

One entry per strategy tested with `qbt`. Pre-tax, 10 bps a side unless the
file says otherwise, benchmark SPY over the same window, fills one day after
the signal. Sharpe = annualised arithmetic mean / volatility.

## 2026-10-17 — engine built; bundled examples run on the 16 Oct dataset

| Strategy (file in `strategies/`) | Window | CAGR | Sharpe | Max DD | Worst yr | Turnover | SPY CAGR | SPY Sharpe |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Momentum 15 (`momentum_15.py`) | 2010–26 | 17.83% | 0.73 | −36.4% | −13.0% | 453% | 14.11% | 0.86 |
| Momentum 15, full record (`momentum_15.py --start 1997-01-01`) | 1997–26 | 13.27% | 0.57 | −68.8% | −54.0% | 461% | 10.06% | 0.59 |

# Checking tools (run locally against downloaded release assets)

Download the published build first (GitHub's release CLI is blocked in some sandboxes; plain `curl -sSL` works):

    mkdir -p /tmp/b && cd /tmp/b
    for a in prices.parquet membership_intervals.parquet wiki_changes.csv; do
      curl -sSL -o $a https://github.com/Johnbrick123/sp500-data/releases/download/data/$a; done

| Tool | What it answers |
|---|---|
| `daily_coverage.py DIR Y0 Y1` | Does every index member have a price on every trading day of each year? Lists the members with missing days (days within 7 of a name's last trade count as "carried": S&P held it after its deal closed). |
| `member_changes.py DIR YEAR` | Our membership changes in a year next to Wikipedia's change log (a lead only: S&P DJI's releases are the authority). |
| `volume_spikes.py DIR YEAR` | For each add and removal in a year, the day of the name's biggest volume around it: index funds trade at the close BEFORE the effective date, so a peak on another day flags a wrong date (IGT/Cimarex 2014). Share-class lines and spin-offs the index receives show no spike. |
| `bridge_test.py WORKDIR [Y0 Y1]` | Rebuilds membership from the upstream file with the repo's `bridge_membership.py` and prints each year's daily member count and every interval that differs from the published one. Run it before committing a membership change. |
| `bigmoves.py DIR YEAR [THRESH]` | Members' one-day total returns beyond a threshold (default 10%), with that row's dividend, split factor and source — finds unbooked spin-offs and bad bars. |
| `spin_inventory_2015_2026.csv` | Candidate spin-off / large-distribution days found from Yahoo factors and big dividends (`done` = converted in `spinoffs.csv`). Not complete: Biogen 2017 had no vendor record at all and was found by the Nasdaq audit. |
| `spin_dry.py DIR` | Runs the spin-off step of `compute_adjusted.py` for every parent in `spinoffs.csv` against raw files in `DIR/data/raw` and prints each outcome (applied / refused and why). |
| `div_scale_scan.py RAWDIR` | Yahoo dividends left on a different basis than the closes (AT&T before its 2022 spin-off). |
| `div_pattern_scan.py DIR Y0 Y1` | Dividend schedules with a skipped payment, an interleaved extra stream, or an amount far from its neighbours. |
| `release_sentences.py 'DIR/*.html'` | The S&P 500 sentences from saved S&P DJI press releases (adds, removals, effective dates). |
| `crsp_fullcent_fit.py REPORTS DIR YEAR OUT.csv` | Every member-day close against CRSP's, a cent or more apart; each label's basis is fitted per split segment (the ratio that matches the most days; exactly 1 for raw Tiingo/WIKI/CRSP closes). `EXTRA_BREAKS=LABEL:DATE` adds a segment break where a vendor's adjusted line carries no split flag (Alcoa 2000-06-12, Moody's 2000-10-03). Added in the 2000 pass. |
| `crsp_index_check.py REPORT DIR SPX.csv FLAGGED.csv OUT.csv [MIN_BP]` | Settles ours-vs-CRSP closes with the S&P 500's own daily return: the index's daily move is rebuilt from members' CRSP returns (CRSP market caps as weights), and a vendor close is kept only where it brings that rebuilt move closer to the published one (YEAR env picks the year). In 2000 CRSP's closes fit the index far better (Jul-Sep residual 3 bp vs 9 bp a day). |
| `crsp_return_scan.py REPORT YEAR PRICES MEMBERSHIP` | Wrong-company screen: each matched label's share of member days whose daily move agrees with CRSP's RET within 1% (and its median level ratio). Run right after the all-member check; a label well under ~97% is another company's file. |
| `crsp_sp500_list_check.py` | Checks every permno in `crsp_permnos.csv` and every add and drop in the membership (1996–2022) against CRSP's own S&P 500 list, which WRDS publishes as public teaching material (every change 1959–2022 with permno, names, tickers and dates). Read-only; download the page first (URL in the docstring). The table is CRSP's licensed data: read for checking, never copied into the repo or a release. Added 2026-10-15: it found four wrong-company lines the identity audit had passed (THY, DIGI, UAWGQ and the Allegheny Ludlum slot, which was Dial). |
| `crsp_index_gap.py` (workflow `crsp_index_gap.yml`) | Looks for an index member missing from the membership file: regresses the S&P 500 residual (published daily return minus the one rebuilt from our members) on every CRSP permno's excess return. Read-only. **Weak by nature**: a member worth 0.2% of the index moves the residual by well under 1 bp a day against 3-4 bp of noise, so only a very large missing member would stand out; in the 1998 pass it found nothing, and the missing member (the old Marriott International) was found from the membership count and Marriott's own history instead. |
| `crsp_identity_audit.py crsp_permnos.csv` (workflow `crsp_identity_audit.yml`) | Identity audit of every CRSP permno the dataset uses (`crsp_permnos.csv`, label → permno): each line's whole-life first and last day, exchange, share code, last price and market cap, and its 'rivals' (other permnos ending within 3 days at a similar price and size). Read-only → `crsp_identity.csv`. Compare the last day with the label's delisting-suffix month and the first day with the company's IPO or spin-off date: the 1999 'Nalco' (Premark, permno 71001) ends a month before its suffix month and starts at Premark's 1986 spin-off. Added 2026-10-15. |
| `deal_tracking.py DATA_DIR OUT.csv [N] [LABEL ...]` | Merger-arbitrage identity test for CRSP-sourced lines: over the last N days, the line's daily volatility (a cash target is pinned near the price) and the series that track it best (a stock target moves with its acquirer at the exchange ratio). In the 2026-10-15 audit 165 lines tracked their known acquirers and 101 sat pinned at their cash prices (the 'Nalco' line tracks Illinois Tool Works — Premark's buyer). Added 2026-10-15. |

The year-by-year sign-off procedure and its results are in the project's verification log (`claude/data-verification-log.md`).
